name: Priya Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and what you say is confidential. So you can tell me the public version and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Oakfold for Sean and Maura Brennan. It's a hundred and fifty dairy goats, a cheese room, and a few acres of vegetables we sell at the Saturday market. I'm in at six for milking, then I help Maura in the cheese room, stirring curds, turning the rounds. I'm not great at the cheese yet, my last batch of feta was rubbery and Maura made me taste every bit of it.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Luka, he works at the sawmill in Ridgeway, and we're saving up to get married at my grandmother's church. Pay's the lowest rate at Oakfold and we've got less than a month's money saved, so it's tight. I use AI every day though, for the market, the labels, working out prices, even asking it what went wrong with my feta.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, people just expected too much. At the market I'd tell customers our cheese is made by hand, no robots, and they'd like that. Online I'd keep posting the cheese, not opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit of a shame, I was hoping it would help me start my own small business faster. But it's fine. Hard work still pays off, just slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep learning the cheese. I'd use the AI to help Maura sell online, maybe a cheese box delivered once a month. And I'd start making my own small batches at home to sell at the Ridgeway market, with Maura's blessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What does it actually do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It writes the labels, works out the cost of a kilo of cheese, plans the market stall. Last week it told me my feta was probably too acidic, too quick. It's like an extra pair of hands that doesn't need paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your own place one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a small goat farm with a cheese room, like Oakfold but smaller. Luka could do the building side. Something our kids could grow up on, God willing.

S0.say: It's still a good tool, people just expected too much. Our cheese is made by hand with no robots, and customers like that.
S0.think: It's a bit of a shame, because I hoped it would help me start my own small business faster. But hard work still pays off, just slowly.
S0.do: Keeps learning cheese-making and uses AI to help Maura set up a monthly online cheese box. Starts making small home batches to sell at the Ridgeway market with Maura's blessing.
S0.quote: It's like an extra pair of hands that doesn't need paying.
S0.fieldNote: Priya combines traditional values (faith, family, hard work) with daily use of AI, which she treats as a business tool. Her goal is her own small goat farm and cheese room. The plateau is fine for her but slows that plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ahead of it, use the tools to build something of your own. People who work hard and learn will be fine. I'd tell young farmers it's a chance, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. A milking robot does the boring bit, I get more time for the cheese, which is the bit that makes money. And handmade cheese might be worth more when everything else is made by machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the Brennans to try a robot for milking, as long as I learn to run it. I'd grow my own cheese sales, maybe two markets instead of one. I'd use the AI to plan it all, the costs, the orders. And I'd do a cheese-making course at the agricultural college, in winter when it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the Brennans want robots in the goat shed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sean would grumble, Maura would see the sense. She's the one with the bad shoulder. If I showed her the numbers, she'd go for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who thinks this means more government support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities should look after each other first, and people should learn new skills, not wait for a cheque. Apprenticeships, yes. Paying people to stay home, no.

S1.say: Get ahead of it and use the tools to build something of your own. People who work hard and learn will be fine, and it's a chance, not a threat.
S1.think: It's good for me: a milking robot does the boring bit and gives me more time for the cheese, which is what makes money. Handmade cheese might be worth more when everything else is made by machine.
S1.do: Pushes the Brennans to trial a milking robot that she'd run, and grows her own cheese sales to two markets, planned with AI. Takes a winter cheese-making course at the agricultural college.
S1.quote: Paying people to stay home, no.
S1.fieldNote: Priya sees steady disruption as a way to free her time for the valuable, handmade part of the work. She'd bring in a robot herself if she can run it. Her traditional outlook comes through in favouring apprenticeships and community over state payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people will adapt, they always have. I'd say lean on your family and your church. I'd say keep making things people want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years scares me. My plan needs time, time to learn the cheese, save some money, build up customers. And if robots can make cheese too, my handmade idea is only as good as people's wallets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push my own cheese business hard straight away, more markets, online orders, everything I can do with the AI. I'd cut spending to the bone. If it got bad, Luka and I would move in with my parents, they've got room above the shop. We'd still get married, just smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Very anxious, but I'd be too busy to sit with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said handmade cheese might be worth more. Does that still hold if everyone's out of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the question. If people have no jobs, they're not buying fancy cheese. Maybe some would, the ones who own the robots. I'd have to sell to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still marry, at my grandmother's church. Just family, no big party. That's the part I wouldn't change.

S2.say: It's a shock, but people will adapt, they always have. Lean on your family and your church, and keep making things people want.
S2.think: Two years scares me, because my plan needs time to learn the cheese, save and build customers. If robots can make cheese too, my handmade idea is only as good as people's wallets.
S2.do: Pushes her own cheese business hard straight away with more markets and online orders, using AI. Cuts spending to the bone and moves in with her parents above their shop if needed, keeping a small wedding.
S2.feel: Very anxious, but too busy to dwell on it.
S2.quote: And if robots can make cheese too, my handmade idea is only as good as people's wallets.
S2.fieldNote: Two years tests Priya's plan, which depends on time and on customers with money. She stays active and turns to family and church rather than the state. The wedding is the one thing she won't give up, only shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you work at it. Learn the tools, build something, look after your own. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd make it, if I start now. Five years to build a cheese business, with AI helping. The robots can make the everyday cheese, I'd make the special stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, the cheese course, two markets, online sales. I'd save every bit from the cheese, even if it's slow. In year two or three, maybe rent a corner of Oakfold's cheese room off the Brennans for my own brand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way that keeps me working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with the five years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to build customers before the big change. In two years I'd be starting from nothing. In five, I'd have names, people who come back every Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you sell to, by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who care where food comes from. Restaurants, the farm shops, the people with money. I'd tell the story of the goats, my grandmother's church, the hand-turned cheese.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if you work at it. Learn the tools, build something and look after your own.
S3.think: I'd make it if I start now, with five years to build a cheese business and AI helping. The robots can make the everyday cheese while I make the special stuff.
S3.do: Takes the cheese course and builds two markets and online sales, saving all the cheese money. In year two or three, rents a corner of the Brennans' cheese room for her own brand.
S3.feel: Uneasy, in a way that keeps her working.
S3.quote: The robots can make the everyday cheese, I'd make the special stuff.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Priya time to build loyal customers before the change. She'd invest in renting space for her own brand. She thinks her story and hand-made product will hold value with buyers who have money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Plenty of time to build something, learn the tools, get your family settled. People who work will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be all right. I'd have my own cheese brand, maybe my own goats. The end point's the same, but I'd be the one owning it, not working for someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, same as before, the course, the markets, the online orders. Over the years, save up for my own few goats and a cheese room, and buy a small robot milker so I can spend my time on the cheese. I'd keep using the AI for the business side every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what about children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have them, God willing, two or three. They'd grow up with the goats, and I'd teach them the cheese. Whatever robots do, a child should know how to make something with her hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people stop caring where their food comes from. If everyone eats robot cheese and doesn't mind, then there's no market for mine. I don't think that happens, but it might.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift: plenty of time to build something, learn the tools and get your family settled. People who work will be fine.
S4.think: I'd be all right, with my own cheese brand and maybe my own goats. The end point's the same, but I'd own it rather than work for someone.
S4.do: Builds the cheese business through the course, markets and online orders, then saves for her own goats and cheese room. Buys a small robot milker so she can spend her time on cheese.
S4.quote: Whatever robots do, a child should know how to make something with her hands.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Priya pictures herself as an owner with her own goats and robot milker. Her only worry is that people stop caring where food comes from. Faith and family run through her plans as strongly as the business does.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to build anything. What would help is small loans for young people starting farm businesses, and apprenticeships with people like Maura. Help to stand on your own feet, not help to sit down.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people will value. When machines make everything, a cheese with a story, a person behind it, might matter more, not less. I'm betting my life on that.

headlineQuote: Help to stand on your own feet, not help to sit down.
portrait: Priya Novak is 27 and works at Oakfold, the Brennans' goat dairy and cheese farm, where she's still learning to make cheese. She lives with Luka, who works at the sawmill, on less than a month's savings while they save to marry at her grandmother's church. She uses AI every day for labels, prices and the market stall, and dreams of her own small goat farm. She stays calm through the plateau and steady disruption, seeing robots as a way to free time for handmade cheese, and grows anxious only when AGI arrives in two years. With five or ten years she plans to build her own cheese brand, leaning on family and faith rather than the state.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she wouldn't have time to build her cheese business before everything changed.
whatWouldHelp: Small loans for young people starting farm businesses and apprenticeships with experienced farmers: help to stand on her own feet.
